title: The Hare and the Tortoise
originalTitle: Λαγωὸς καὶ χελώνη · Lagōos kai chelōnē
place: A country road in ancient Greece
sourceAuthor: Aesop; selected and retold by Joseph Jacobs
note: Joseph Jacobs’s public-domain text is reproduced directly; only page divisions are editorial. The fable is commonly catalogued as Perry 226.

rights.basis: The 1894 source edition is identified as public domain in the United States by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: A tortoise approaches an olive-wreathed finish while a hare wakes beneath a tree.

pageArt.alt: Tortoise walks steadily past Hare, who sleeps beneath an olive tree beside the ancient Greek road.
Tortoise crosses the olive-wreathed finish just before the astonished Hare arrives.

scenes: The Hare was once boasting of his speed before the other animals. “I have never yet been beaten,” said he, “when I put forth my full speed. I challenge any one here to race with me.”
The Tortoise said quietly, “I accept your challenge.”
“That is a good joke,” said the Hare; “I could dance round you all the way.”
“Keep your boasting till you’ve beaten,” answered the Tortoise. “Shall we race?”
So a course was fixed and a start was made. The Hare darted almost out of sight at once, but soon stopped and, to show his contempt for the Tortoise, lay down to have a nap.
The Tortoise plodded on and plodded on, and when the Hare awoke from his nap, he saw the Tortoise just near the winning-post and could not run up in time to save the race. Then said the Tortoise:
